ha_title: Home Assistant: decide what AI agents may do
ha_intro: Home-Mandate for Home Assistant sits between your AI agents and your home. For every device and action it decides: allow, ask or deny – with approval on your phone, an emergency stop and a tamper-evident log.
ha_status_text: Home-Mandate for Home Assistant is not final yet. Expect rough edges, read the [limits of this version](https://github.com/home-mandate/ha-home-mandate#limits-of-this-version) and keep backups.
ha_why_title: Why a token is not enough
ha_why_text_1: An AI agent that holds a Home Assistant token can do everything that token can: unlock the front door, disarm the alarm, open the garage. A prompt injection in an e-mail or a web page the agent reads is enough to make it try. Exposing devices to assistants only knows on or off – no time windows, no limits on values, no confirmation before an action.
ha_why_text_2: Home-Mandate keeps Home Assistant’s credentials to itself. Every agent gets its own identity and its own [mandate](/glossary/), and every request is decided by fixed rules outside the language model – so no agent can talk itself into more. [Why mandates?](/why/)
ha_how_agent_body: It connects over MCP and signs in with OAuth 2.1. It never sees a Home Assistant token.
ha_how_check_body: Home-Mandate looks up the device and evaluates the agent’s mandate: allow, ask or deny.
ha_how_ask_body: With ask, your phone shows Allow and Deny in the Companion app. No answer means no.
ha_how_ha_body: Only an allowed or confirmed action reaches Home Assistant. Everything lands in the audit log.
ha_how_rules: The decision is made by the reference evaluator of the [Home-Mandate Specification](/spec/v0/), never by a language model. What is not allowed is denied. Devices an agent may not read do not exist for it: they are neither listed nor named in errors.
ha_example_lead: A mandate for a voice assistant that helps around the house could look like this. Home-Mandate brings three templates to start from.
ha_example_allow_1: Switch lights in the living room and kitchen
ha_example_allow_3: Set the heating, to 22 °C at most
ha_example_deny_2: Anything not named in the mandate
ha_try_text: In the playground you write a mandate and see right away which requests it allows, asks about or denies.
ha_feature_rules: Allow, ask or deny per device, area, category and action – with time windows, weekdays, value limits (brightness, temperature, position, volume) and a limit on actions per hour.
ha_feature_critical: Critical actions – unlocking, opening a gate or garage door, disarming the alarm, running scripts, camera snapshots – need an approval even where a rule allows them, unless the rule says otherwise explicitly.
ha_feature_approval: Approval requests go to the phones of the people you choose, through the Home Assistant Companion app.
ha_feature_stop: An emergency stop halts every agent at once; single agents can be revoked.
ha_feature_log: Every decision, approval and change is written to a hash-chained audit log with signed checkpoints.
ha_feature_token: Agents get short-lived tokens bound to Home-Mandate; no agent is admitted without a Home Assistant administrator.
ha_feature_ui: Web UI in English and German, in the Home Assistant sidebar; administration on the command line as well.
ha_install_1_body: Home Assistant OS 2026.9 or later on amd64 or aarch64 – or Home Assistant Container with Docker or Podman Compose. The Companion app on the phone of everyone who should answer approval requests.
ha_install_2_body: On Home Assistant OS, add the repository below in the app store (Settings → Apps → App store → ⋮ → Repositories) and install Home-Mandate. With Home Assistant Container, run it with the Compose file next to Home Assistant.
ha_install_3_title: Set up approvers and a mandate
ha_install_3_body: Choose who answers approval requests, mark critical devices and start from one of the templates.
ha_install_4_body: Claude Desktop, Claude Code, claude.ai, ChatGPT or another MCP client signs in; a Home Assistant administrator admits it and picks its mandate.

ha_remote_text_1: Most agents do not run in your home network, so they need to reach Home-Mandate over HTTPS. Home-Mandate speaks TLS 1.3 only. On Home Assistant OS it uses a certificate in /ssl, for example from the Let’s Encrypt or DuckDNS app, and needs a TLS passthrough or a port forward.
ha_remote_text_2: In container mode, Home-Mandate can also run behind your own reverse proxy: there are [guides for Traefik, nginx, Nginx Proxy Manager and Caddy](https://github.com/home-mandate/ha-home-mandate/blob/main/docs/deploy/reverse-proxy.md).
ha_conformance_text: Home-Mandate for Home Assistant embeds the reference evaluator of the specification and runs its conformance cases on every change. Which version and which classes it passes is in the [list of implementations](/implementations/), checked against the published reports.
ha_faq_agents_q: Which AI agents work with it?
ha_faq_agents_a: Every agent that speaks MCP over HTTPS and signs in with OAuth 2.1 – for example Claude Desktop, Claude Code, claude.ai and ChatGPT. Clients without browser sign-in can pair with a code.
ha_faq_assist_q: Does it replace exposing devices to Assist?
ha_faq_assist_a: No. Assist keeps working as before. Home-Mandate is the way in for AI agents that should not hold a Home Assistant token – with rules per agent instead of one list for all.
ha_faq_official_q: Is this part of Home Assistant?
ha_faq_official_a: No. Home-Mandate for Home Assistant is an independent open-source project and implements the open Home-Mandate Specification. It uses Home Assistant’s public interfaces and asks nothing of Home Assistant itself.
ha_faq_platforms_q: What about openHAB, ioBroker or other platforms?
ha_faq_platforms_a: The specification is open to every platform. Implementations for other platforms are welcome and appear in the [list of implementations](/implementations/).
